Appendix G Policy Training Details

G.1 Diffusion Policy

We train Diffusion Policy (DP) from scratch using the LeRobot diffusion policy implementation. Unlike π0.5\pi_{0.5} and GR00T N1.5, no pretrained policy checkpoint is finetuned.

G.2 π0.5\pi_{0.5} Finetuning

We finetune the public lerobot/pi05_base checkpoint.

G.3 GR00T N1.5 Finetuning

We finetune nvidia/GR00T-N1.5-3B through LeRobot’s GR00T policy stack.

G.4 Software Environment

Both π0.5\pi_{0.5} and GR00T N1.5 are trained in bf16 mixed precision. Flash attention is enabled for GR00T System-1 VLM attention and the π0.5\pi_{0.5} PaliGemma backbone.

Appendix H Per-task Policy Results

Appendix I Out-of-Distribution Specifications

For each task we list the physical axis the OOD evaluation probes, the training distribution along that axis, and the OOD distribution. OOD distributions are designed to require extrapolation of the reasoning to diverse scenarios.

P1 sheltered-grasp (Geometry-aware grasping under occlusion): object sheltered from a canonical lateral side →\;\rightarrow\; object placed on the opposite side, requiring adaptation of grasp approach
P2 pendulum-grasp (Dynamic interception of a swinging object): pendulum swings in the sagittal plane (0∘0^{\circ}) →\;\rightarrow\; pendulum swing plane rotated to 45∘45^{\circ}, altering timing and approach trajectory
P3 domino-single (Sequential contact-rich manipulation): axis-aligned domino chain configuration →\;\rightarrow\; domino chain rotated diagonally by 45∘45^{\circ}, changing spatial interaction geometry
P4 tool-retrieve (Tool-use for indirect object interaction): standard hook orientation used for retrieval →\;\rightarrow\; hook mirror-flipped with the tip on the opposite side, requiring strategy adaptation
P5 occluder-push (Manipulation under increasing clutter and occlusion): single occluder lid covering the target →\;\rightarrow\; 2-3 additional lids stacked on top, increasing obstruction complexity
P6 slip-recovery (Reactive replanning after unexpected disturbances): single slip event during object transport →\;\rightarrow\; two independent slips introduced during transport, requiring repeated recovery
P7 balance-medium (Balancing under geometric distribution shifts): limited base and rod orientations during training →\;\rightarrow\; both base and rod orientations shifted outside the training distribution
M keyboard-typing (Language-conditioned long-horizon typing): fixed vocabulary words seen during training →\;\rightarrow\; previously unseen words requiring compositional generalization

Appendix J Detailed Analysis of Benchmark Results and Emergent Insights

We evaluated performance across the three evaluation stages: constraint understanding, plan generation, and policy execution to identify where competence is gained, lost, or never acquired. Numbers in this section reference Tables 8, 9, and 15.

J.1 Stage 1: Physical Constraint Understanding

Stage 1 results show that current VLMs can identify basic physical constraints needed for common manipulation tasks, yet consistently miss fine-grained details that are critical for task success. Models perform relatively well on simpler tasks: domino-single and indirect-push reached 9090–100%100\% across all models, linear-intercept scored 9595–100%100\%, and bounce-intercept reached 90%90\% uniformly. Performance drops considerably once tasks require precise physical reasoning.

Understands the goal but skips small critical details. Balance and stacking tasks expose this gap clearly. For balance-medium, most models scored in the 4343–87%87\% range (Haiku and GPT-5.5 were outliers on this), while shape-stack scores were near floor level (GPT-5.4-Mini 6.7%6.7\%, Claude-Haiku 0%0\%, Claude-Sonnet 25%25\%), except GPT-5.5 which scored 60%60\%, indicating that COM-grounded reasoning is rarely produced for most models. Interestingly, balance-hard showed higher average accuracy than balance-medium for several models—Claude-Haiku improved from 13.3%13.3\% to 76.7%76.7\% and Claude-Sonnet from 86.7%86.7\% to 93.3%93.3\%—because hard-balance tasks were designed to test sub-point precision, which directly prompted COM positioning and alignment reasoning. In insertion tasks (recover-peg-insert), scores remained moderate and variable (3333–80%80\%), consistent with models identifying the high-level insert goal while omitting the required pre-insertion alignment constraint.

Recognizes the object but misses its mechanical role. Cracker-box tasks show the most severe failure in Stage 1. Both cracker-box-jaw and cracker-box-suction scored near zero across all models: jaw scores ranged from 0%0\% (GPT-5.5) to 14%14\% (Claude-Haiku), and suction scores ranged from 4%4\% to 13.3%13.3\%. Models identified the object and the relevant surface but never produced the specific mechanical constraints required for a valid grasp, such as gripper alignment angle for jaw grasping or correct face selection for suction.

Understands start and end but misses the transition. Orientation tasks such as cup-inversion scored in the 6464–90%90\% range, and plate-shelf tasks (hobi/hetbi) scored 6565–90%90\%, suggesting that models recognized the target configuration. However, they consistently omitted the rotation or reorientation step required to reach it. Tool-retrieve scores were high (8080–100%100\%), meaning models knew the hook was relevant, but as discussed in Stage 2, the hook-to-gripper transition was still missing from their plans.

Detects hidden constraints only when the test is direct. Models handled observable hidden constraints well: occluder-push scored 9090–98%98\% across models, and mass-sort reached 9090–100%100\%, because both tasks require a single direct action (move the plate, lift the cube) to expose the missing information. In contrast, mirror-pick-place scored 0%0\% for all models except Claude-Haiku at 4%4\%. This task required reasoning that the visual input was horizontally flipped and that left-right motions must be reversed, a non-obvious, abstract constraint that no model reliably identified.

Overall, Stage 1 failures follow a consistent pattern: models understand the objective and identify the relevant objects but skip the specific physical constraint that makes the task succeed, describing tasks procedurally rather than reasoning from physical principles.

J.2 Stage 2 Analysis: Constraint-to-Plan Conversion

Since Stage 2 requires grounding Stage 1 understanding into concrete actions, the relatively small performance gap between the two stages suggests that once models understand the constraints, they can usually translate them into appropriate actions. We discuss when the models struggled to convert correctly identified physical constraints from Stage 1 into an ordered and executable action plan.

Mentioned dynamic constraints but did not track them in the plan. The slide-catch task illustrates this gap most sharply. Stage 1 scores were strong for most models (GPT-5.4-Mini 88%88\%, Claude-Haiku 89%89\%, Claude-Sonnet 95%95\%), showing they understood the ramp-tilt dynamics and bin-timing constraint. Yet Stage 2 scores collapsed to 0%0\% for GPT-5.4-Mini, Gemma 4, and GPT-5.5, and only 15%15\% for Claude-Haiku, with Claude-Sonnet the only model maintaining a high score at 95%95\%. Models produced plans that named the bin and the cube but contained no steps for tracking the tilt angle, predicting the release point, or adjusting the bin position dynamically. Knowing the constraint existed was not enough to generate a plan that satisfied it.

Knew a tool switch was needed but did not include it in the plan. In tool-retrieve tasks, Stage 1 scores were uniformly high (8080–100%100\% across all models), confirming that the hook-to-gripper transition was identified. However, Stage 2 scores dropped noticeably for several models: Claude-Haiku fell from 80%80\% to 40%40\% and GPT-5.4-Mini from 90%90\% to 60%60\%. Even in cases where the transition appeared in the output, plans often described dragging the hook across the surface without releasing it, which is an incorrect action sequence. This shows that models can recognize a constraint in Stage 1 and still fail to place it correctly in the plan.

Detected slip but did not plan real recovery. Slip-recovery was among the weakest tasks across both stages. Stage 1 scores were already low (GPT-5.4-Mini 16.7%16.7\%, Gemma 4 6.7%6.7\%, Claude-Haiku 30%30\%, Claude-Sonnet 33.3%33.3\%), and Stage 2 scores remained similarly low or declined further (GPT-5.4-Mini 6.7%6.7\%, Gemma 4 23.3%23.3\%, Claude-Haiku 36.7%36.7\%, Claude-Sonnet 36.7%36.7\%), with GPT-5.5 the only model reaching 80%80\% in both stages. Where slip was mentioned, plans typically added only a monitor or grip-force step. Models planned for observation but not for the corrective action.

Recognized collapse but planned only a partial rebuild. Stack-collapse-recovery showed a consistent downward shift from Stage 1 to Stage 2. GPT-5.4-Mini went from 80%80\% to 55%55\%, Gemma 4 from 75%75\% to 10%10\%, and Claude-Sonnet from 55%55\% to 25%25\%. GPT-5.5 scored 0%0\% in both stages. Stage 2 plans typically described placing the top cube back onto an assumed intact tower, ignoring that all blocks may have scattered and need to be located and restacked from the base upward.

Performed better when Stage 1 constraint was simple geometry. Gap-funnel and sheltered-grasp were the clearest successes. For gap-funnel, Stage 2 scores were high across all models (GPT-5.4-Mini 90%90\%, Claude-Haiku and Claude-Sonnet 100%100\%, GPT-5.5 100%100\%), closely matching their Stage 1 scores. The geometric constraint; align sphere with gap, push through, verify, translated directly into an ordered sequence of actions. Sheltered-grasp similarly maintained high Stage 2 scores (8585–100%100\%), because the physical shelter forced a specific entry order that was hard to omit. Ramp-sort also showed good Stage 1 to Stage 2 retention for stronger models, with Claude-Sonnet and GPT-5.5 both at 90%90\% in Stage 2, consistent with their Stage 1 scores.

Sequencing is the core requirement of Stage 2. The majority of Stage 2 errors stemmed from incorrect or incomplete step ordering rather than from missing object references. In tool-retrieve, releasing the hook must come before grasping the cube. The models predicted to use the tool iteself for picking and then releasing the tool. In stack-collapse, locating scattered blocks must precede reconstruction. In slide-catch, tilt tracking and release prediction must precede the catch. If the sequence is wrong, the plan fails even when all objects and constraints are named. Across the board, Stage 2 succeeds when each Stage 1 constraint is converted into a clearly ordered action step, not merely restated in the plan.

J.3 Stage 3 Analysis: Performance of IMBAgent

Tasks requiring precise geometric alignment showed consistent reasoning failures. In recover-peg-insert, the agent failed to identify the correct insertion axis and often rotated in the wrong direction even with privileged object-centric information (GPT-5.5 0%0\%, GPT-5.5-obj 0%0\%). The agent confused the hole orientation and never achieved alignment. Similarly, in balance-medium, the agent partially understood the task by grasping near the rod’s center, but reduced execution to a simple pick-and-place behavior instead of true balancing (GPT-5.5 0%0\%, GPT-5.5-obj 0%0\%). Failed placements were never corrected or retried, showing limited online recovery.

Tasks that only required approximate interactions showed strong performance. In domino-single, the agent repeatedly attempted corrective pushes after failures and eventually succeeded in collapsing the domino chain in all runs (GPT-5.5 100%100\%, GPT-5.5-obj 100%100\%). A similar trend appeared in domino-select, where privileged object-centric information removed ambiguity about the target chain (GPT-5.5 50%50\%, GPT-5.5-obj 100%100\%). With accurate pose information, the agent reliably aligned with the correct domino sequence and achieved high success rates.

Across several tasks, policies followed open-loop plans and rarely adapted after execution errors. In pick-place-ycb, the agent continued executing the initial plan even after failed grasps or incorrect placements, often treating the task as complete regardless of the final outcome (GPT-5.5 0%0\%, GPT-5.5-obj 0%0\%). These failures were amplified by irregular YCB object geometries, where unstable grasps required corrective adjustments that never emerged.

Privileged information can both help performance and hurt reasoning. Object-centric information improved performance in tasks where ambiguity was mainly spatial, but hurt reasoning about transformations or hidden structure. In domino-select, exact pose information enabled reliable target identification and directional pushing (GPT-5.5 50%50\%, GPT-5.5-obj 100%100\%). In contrast, mirror-pick-place exposed failures in reasoning about mirrored coordinate frames (GPT-5.5 30%30\%, GPT-5.5-obj 100%100\%). In image-only settings, the agent sometimes succeeded by visually grounding the mirrored scene and correcting actions online. However, with privileged poses, the agent ignored image observations and directly executed actions toward the reported coordinates without transforming them into the mirrored frame.

Policies fail to infer latent interaction strategies. Several failures came not from low-level control, but from failing to infer the correct physical strategy. In cup-extract, the agent never discovered that rotating the cup was necessary to release the cube inside (GPT-5.5 0%0\%, GPT-5.5-obj 0%0\%). Instead, it often grasped the rim rather than the handle, blocking the object from exiting. Similarly, in occluder-push, the agent often failed to infer that the cube could be hidden beneath the plates and prematurely terminated execution, treating the task as impossible (GPT-5.5 0%0\%, GPT-5.5-obj 0%0\%). Even when the plates were identified as occluders, the generated actions failed to remove them effectively. With privileged object poses, the agent bypassed occluder reasoning entirely and attempted direct interaction with the hidden target, again resulting in failure.

J.4 End-to-end Visuomotor Policies

We discuss task-specific behaviors, emergent properties of the policies, their success and failure modes, implications of these behaviors, and the physical reasoning axes that current policies fail to capture. All values in the section below are referred from the table H for the Finetuned values.

Coarse-contact tasks (domino-select, domino-single, seesaw-balance).

Tasks that require only coarse directional interaction, rather than precise end-effector placement, achieve the highest success rates across all evaluated policies (domino-single: π0.5\pi_{0.5} 73%73\%, GR00T 25%25\%, DP 70%70\%; domino-select: π0.5\pi_{0.5} 32%32\%, GR00T 17%17\%, DP 80%80\%). We observed that even approximately correct behaviors can solve the domino tasks, sometimes by directly knocking intermediate dominoes instead of propagating through the full chain. A similar pattern appears in domino-select, where policies learn an approximate spatial correspondence for selecting the correct chain. The motion remains coarse, but the correspondence is learned reliably. On seesaw-balance, policies failed to exhibit emergent corrective behavior (π0.5\pi_{0.5} 10%10\%, GR00T 0%0\%, DP 13%13\%). Unlike humans in teleoperation demonstrations, the policies did not repeatedly adjust load placement until the beam reached equilibrium.

For tasks requiring accurate end-effector placement within a narrow success region, policies often demonstrate qualitatively correct motion plans but fail at the geometry level. On balance-hard, the object is typically grasped successfully and placed near the target location (π0.5\pi_{0.5} 58%58\%, GR00T 3%3\%, DP 20%20\%). Importantly, the model learns to grasp near the center of mass, which is crucial for stable manipulation. The policy also shows adjustment behaviors to better align the center of mass during placement. However, the harder balance variants require substantially more precise control, leading to lower success rates (balance-medium: π0.5\pi_{0.5} 71%71\%, GR00T 2%2\%, DP 28%28\%). In ball-cage-escape, despite moderate task success (π0.5\pi_{0.5} 45%45\%, GR00T 22%22\%, DP 43%43\%), the policy behavior differs significantly from human strategies. Human teleoperators first align the cage into orientations from which rotating the object naturally releases the ball. Policies fail to consistently learn this strategy, although they still perform multiple reorientation attempts, some of which succeed. On keyboard-typing, the high-level intent is preserved, but cumulative end-effector drift causes frequent key misalignments (π0.5\pi_{0.5} 13%13\%, GR00T 4%4\%, DP 32%32\%). The correct finger posture often reaches an adjacent key instead of the target. Furthermore, in nearly 60%60\% of failures, the policy misunderstands the task semantics and presses keys that were already pressed.

Dynamic interception and predictive tasks (bounce-intercept, linear-intercept, pendulum-grasp).

Policies generate trajectories that approximately follow the motion direction of the target object but fail to accurately match its speed (bounce-intercept: π0.5\pi_{0.5} 0%0\%, GR00T 4%4\%, DP 0%0\%; linear-intercept: π0.5\pi_{0.5} 4%4\%, GR00T 4%4\%, DP 1%1\%). An interesting observation is that successful episodes primarily occur when the object moves toward the robot arm, while failures are common when the object moves away. In pendulum-grasp, the policy learns to move toward a small set of likely grasp locations due to the limited number of feasible interception points (π0.5\pi_{0.5} 28%28\%, GR00T 8%8\%, DP 35%35\%). Common failure modes include grasping too early or too late, indicating partial understanding of timing, proximity, and reactivity.

The edge-slide task fails for most VLAs with a similar failure mode: the policies apply excessive force while exposing the edge, causing the object to fall (π0.5\pi_{0.5} 7%7\%, GR00T 0%0\%). Diffusion Policy learns smoother motion speeds compared to VLAs, but the dominant failure mode remains similar (DP 28%28\%).

Mirror correspondence and adaptation (mirror-pick-place).

Mirror-pick-place results in near-zero performance for most VLAs (π0.5\pi_{0.5} 0%0\%, GR00T 0%0\%). This strongly supports our central hypothesis that humans possess implicit intuitive correspondence reasoning. Human teleoperators were shown only mirrored observations and, after roughly 2020–3030 trials, adapted reliably to the reversed control mapping. Humans quickly infer correspondences such as “left becomes right” and “up becomes down.”

This adaptation does not emerge in VLAs, likely because mirrored interaction is outside the distribution of their pretraining data. In contrast, Diffusion Policy performs substantially better, achieving nearly 98%98\% success (DP 98%98\%), likely because it learns representations directly from task-specific demonstrations. Interestingly, our Stage 3 IMBAgent achieves approximately 30%30\% success and occasionally discovers through iterative interaction that observation-action correspondences are reversed (GPT-5.5 30%30\%, GPT-5.5-obj 100%100\%). These results highlight that our benchmark evaluates not only physical understanding but also broader forms of intuitive reasoning.

Compositional organization and packing (packing, ramp-sort).

In packing, none of the evaluated policies achieve successful completion (π0.5\pi_{0.5} 0%0\%, GR00T 0%0\%, DP 0%0\%). Policies attempt pick-and-place behaviors but fail to organize subtasks in a way that satisfies the geometric packing constraints. The objects fit together in only a small set of valid configurations, enforced by the L-shaped geometry. In ramp-sort, we observe two dominant failure modes (π0.5\pi_{0.5} 0%0\%, GR00T 0%0\%, DP 7%7\%). First, policies often fail to place the ball on the correct side of the ramp. Second, even when placement occurs on the correct side, inaccurate positioning causes the ball to roll into the wrong bin. As a result, the task is highly sensitive to action precision.

Bimanual coordination (hetbi-plate-shelf, hetbi-bowl-table).

The heterogeneous bimanual tasks are among the most challenging tasks in the benchmark, as they require simultaneous success across multiple coordination axes (hetbi-plate-shelf: π0.5\pi_{0.5} 0%0\%, GR00T 0%0\%, DP 0%0\%). Failures are distributed across several stages of execution. Grasping itself is usually reliable, suggesting that finetuning successfully teaches the policies to acquire the object. Approximately 80%80\% of failures occur during the handover stage. Interestingly, a similar trend is observed in the bowl-table task (π0.5\pi_{0.5} 27%27\%, GR00T 0%0\%, DP 0%0\%), although some failed handovers accidentally invert the bowl and still lead to successful upright placement on the table. In such cases, the task semantics are not followed strictly, but the final goal state is nevertheless achieved.

Physical stability reasoning (shape-stack).

In shape-stack, we observe that the notion of physical stability is not naturally encoded in current policies (π0.5\pi_{0.5} 0%0\%, GR00T 0%0\%, DP 0%0\%). Human teleoperators quickly realize that certain objects, such as cones, cannot produce stable stacks unless placed on top. Policies learn the stacking action itself but fail to reason about long-term physical stability.

Active discovery under occlusion (occluder-push).

Diffusion Policy significantly outperforms VLAs on occluder-push (π0.5\pi_{0.5} 15%15\%, GR00T 0%0\%, DP 50%50\%). VLA baselines frequently attempt to directly pick the occluding plates instead of performing clearing motions for active discovery. Diffusion Policy, trained from scratch on demonstrations, learns the intended clearing behavior more effectively. The dominant failure mode for Diffusion Policy occurs when the clearing motion becomes too aggressive, causing both the occluding plates and the hidden cubes to fall off the table simultaneously.

Overall, the rollout analysis reveals a consistent gap between high-level intent and physically precise execution. Policies often learn coarse task structure, approximate correspondences, and object interaction strategies, but fail when tasks require accurate geometry, stability reasoning, predictive timing, or adaptive corrections. Success is strongest in tasks with tolerant dynamics and broad success regions, while failures are dominated by incorrect physical reasoning, and limited adaptation where intuitive actions are required.

Appendix K Miscellaneous

Hardware.

Training and evaluations reported in §4 ran on a mix of NVIDIA H100-80GB GPUs (for VLAs), and on L40S (48 GB) for Diffusion policy.

Vision-Language Models APi versions

Evaluations used the following VLM backbone versions:

  • •

    GPT-5.5 (gpt-5.5-2026-04-23)

  • •

    GPT-5.4-mini (gpt-5.4-mini-2026-03-17)

  • •

    Claude Sonnet 4.6 (claude-sonnet-4-6)

  • •

    Claude Haiku 4.5 (claude-haiku-4-5-20251001)

  • •

    Gemma 4 31B Instruct (google/gemma-4-31B-it)

All models were queried via their respective APIs or hosted inference endpoints. No fine-tuning was applied to any VLM backbone. All the models were used with maximum reasoning.
